items.q: How much does Mailchimp cost per month?
items.a: As of 27 September 2026, Mailchimp sells four plans, and three of them are paid: Free costs $0 and caps at 250 contacts; Essentials starts at $13 a month for up to 500 contacts; Standard starts at $20 for the same 500-contact starting band with more automation and seats; and Premium starts at $350 a month with no fixed seat or contact ceiling. None of those numbers holds as your list grows, because Mailchimp prices every paid plan in contact-count bands, so the same plan costs more once you cross into the next one. A 1,000-contact account on Essentials pays $26.50 a month rather than $13; at 10,000 contacts, a five-person team on Standard pays $135; at 50,000 contacts, an account needing Premium's unlimited seats pays $815. The plan name alone never tells you the real bill; the contact count and, past three or five people, the seat count both do.

items.q: Is Mailchimp actually free, or is that just a trial?
items.a: The Free plan is genuinely free, not a trial. There is no time limit as long as the account stays under Mailchimp's own contact and send caps. Mailchimp's plan-comparison page states the real ceiling as 250 contacts, even though the pricing page's contacts selector groups Free into a wider 0-500 band; go over 250 contacts, or over 500 emails a month (250 a day), and sending pauses until you are back under the limit or you upgrade. Free includes only 1 seat and 1 audience, no role-based access, and no automation flows, SMS/MMS marketing or generative-AI features at all; those need a paid plan. Email support is also limited to your first 30 days on the platform, after which a free account has no direct support channel. The self-serve trial is separate: it applies only to Essentials and Standard, runs 14 days, and needs a card on file before it starts.

items.q: Does Mailchimp charge for unsubscribed contacts?
items.a: Yes. Mailchimp's help center explains that unsubscribed and non-subscribed contacts still count toward your plan's contact limit, the same as active subscribers; only cleaned, pending, archived or deleted contacts are excluded. That matters because Mailchimp bills by contact count in fixed bands: an account sitting at 500 contacts pays $13 a month on Essentials, but if some of those are people who unsubscribed months ago rather than being archived, they are still part of that 500, and one new signup that pushes the real count to 501 moves the bill to $26.50. Archiving a contact, not simply leaving them unsubscribed, is the one action that actually removes them from what you are billed for, and it keeps their history rather than deleting it outright. Reviewing an audience for unsubscribed or long-inactive contacts before a band boundary is crossed is the most direct way to keep the bill where it is.

items.q: What Mailchimp plan does a small business or solo freelancer need?
items.a: It comes down to two things: how many contacts you have, and how many people need their own login. Under 250 contacts, the Free plan works and costs nothing, though it has no automation and email support only for the first 30 days. Past that, Essentials, starting at $13 a month, fits a freelancer or a one- or two-person business; its 3 included seats cover most solo and small setups, and its up to 4 automation-flow steps are enough for a basic welcome or follow-up sequence, though not Mailchimp's full Marketing Automation Flows. A one-person consultancy with about 1,000 contacts pays $26.50 a month on that same plan. The moment a third or fourth person needs shared access to the account, check Essentials' 3-seat cap before assuming it still fits; that is the more common reason a small business outgrows Essentials, not contact-list growth.

items.q: Does Mailchimp offer a discount for paying yearly?
items.a: Only in specific cases. Essentials and Standard show a flat monthly price with no annual option at all until an account reaches 10,000 contacts; below that, there is simply nothing to prepay. Once a Standard account reaches the 10,000-contact band, the same tier that costs $135 a month billed monthly drops to $114.75 a month if paid annually, a real saving, but one that only appears that late. Premium works differently: its annual rate, $297.50 a month against a $350 monthly price, is available from the plan's very first contact tier, not gated behind any contact minimum. Mailchimp's own footnote on annual billing says to contact sales for pricing and eligibility on Premium and 10,000-plus Standard, yet the pricing page itself shows a specific annual figure with a self-serve checkout button at that size regardless. A freelancer or small business on Essentials, in short, has no yearly-billing decision to make until the list grows considerably.

items.q: What happens if a Mailchimp account goes over its plan's limit?
items.a: Every plan card on Mailchimp's pricing and plan-comparison pages carries the same footnote: overage charges apply once you exceed your contact or monthly email-send limit. Neither page states an actual rate for that overage, whether per contact or per email, so a prospective customer has no way to price that risk in advance. On the Free plan, Mailchimp is explicit that sending pauses once you are over your 250-contact or 500-email limit. For Essentials, Standard and Premium, the pages only say overage charges apply; they do not say whether sending also pauses for a paid account the way it does on Free, so do not assume a paid plan protects you from an interruption just because it can absorb a charge. Archiving inactive or unsubscribed contacts, rather than leaving them on the list, is the confirmed way to bring an account back under a cheaper band first.

items.q: Do I need Mailchimp's Premium plan, or is Standard enough?
items.a: Premium removes two caps that Standard has: Standard tops out at 5 seats, and Premium has none, and Mailchimp's comparison page states no fixed maximum contact count for Premium at all, saying to contact sales for a custom plan instead. List size alone rarely forces the upgrade before seats or support do. A 15-person team on a 50,000-contact list needs Premium's unlimited seats regardless of price, paying $815 a month, while the same 50,000 contacts on Standard, if only 5 or fewer people needed logins, would cost $450 instead. Mailchimp's plan-comparison page also states that Standard's own published self-serve ceiling reaches 100,000 contacts at an $800-a-month tier, a figure not re-verified on this record by selecting that exact band. Premium adds phone support and a dedicated onboarding specialist on top of the seat difference, which matters when support responsiveness, not list size or headcount, is the deciding factor.
